one_liner: Java XML parser building a compact offset/length token index, not a tree; beats libxml2 DOM parse, loses XPath.
what_it_does: VTDGen takes the whole document as a byte[] (setDoc) and parse() turns it into a flat index of 64-bit token records plus per-depth element directories. You read it through VTDNav, a single-cursor navigator (toElement(FIRST_CHILD / NEXT_SIBLING / PARENT), getText, toString), and AutoPilot, an XPath 1.0 engine. XMLModifier makes byte-level inserts and deletes without re-serializing, and writeIndex/loadIndex save the parsed index to disk. It is not a DOM and has its own API, so it is not a drop-in for libxml2's xmlDoc tree. The same design is also ported to C, C++ and C#.
how_it_is_fast: It uses non-extractive tokenization, which the project calls Virtual Token Descriptor (VTD). The raw bytes stay in memory undecoded, and each token becomes one 64-bit long: 4-bit type, 8-bit depth, 20-bit length and a 30/32-bit offset. These longs are appended to pooled long[] buffers, so parsing creates no node objects, no strings and almost no GC work. Random access comes from 'location caches': per-depth arrays whose entries pair an element's record index with the index of its first child. The FAQ puts these at about 10% of parse cost and total memory at 1.3-1.5x the document size. End tags are not stored, and setDoc_BR() reuses the buffers across parses.
when_to_use: JVM services that parse many shallow (<255 levels) 100 KB-100 MB documents and read a few fields by navigation, where building DOM objects and the GC they cause is the cost. On bemayer/xml-benchmark its index build posted 0.54-239 ms vs libxml2's 0.87-647 ms, with the caveat that the file sets differ.

Replacing Xerces or JDK DOM in Java code that only reads. On the same page, VTD-XML's DOM Parse time is lower than Xerces's at every size (0.036 vs 0.232 ms at 1KB; 238.9 vs 489.0 ms at 100MB). Again the file sets differ.
Parse once, use many times: save the index with writeIndex() and reload it with loadIndex() so you do not re-tokenize the same large file.
Small edits or fragment cut/paste on large documents (XMLModifier, getElementFragment), which avoids a full DOM round trip and re-serialization.
Files larger than RAM, up to 256 GB, using the extended edition (VTDGenHuge in MEM_MAPPED mode), provided nesting stays at 30 levels or fewer.
when_not_to_use: XPath-heavy workloads. On //*[@id] it was 6.8x-17x slower than libxml2 at every size (3837.5 vs 565.6 ms at 100MB), and slower than Xerces from 1MB up.

Deeply nested XML. The standard edition throws 'Depth exceeds MAX_DEPTH' past 254 levels, and the 256 GB extended edition allows only 30. The standard edition also caps documents at 2 GB, or 1 GB with namespaces on.
Tiny documents or short-lived processes. At 1KB it is 2.8x slower than libxml2, and its peak RSS on the page is 57 MB vs 5.4 MB (JVM baseline).

Anything that needs DTD-declared or external entities, schema validation or a W3C DOM API. The FAQ calls DTD and external entities effectively deprecated, VTDGen parses a DTD but does not resolve declared entities, and a DOM interface is ruled out.
Projects that cannot take GPLv2 plus patent notices and an unmaintained codebase. The last release was 2017, and bugs such as namespace shadowing in getElementFragmentNs (#13) are still open.

integration.form: module (Java jar, Maven Central com.ximpleware:vtd-xml 2.13.4); C, C++ and C# ports are source-drop from the repo
integration.min_toolchain: Java; the FAQ lists Java 1.2 through 8 as tested, and the benchmark ran 2.13.4 on Temurin 21 JRE. The C port builds with a makefile, or with Visual Studio set to 'Compile as C'.
integration.platforms: any JVM; the C, C++ and C# ports cover Linux, Windows and .NET/Mono per the FAQ
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe per instance. VTDNav has exactly one cursor, and AutoPilot moves it. For parallel reads, give each thread its own navigator from duplicateNav() or cloneNav(), which share the read-only XML, VTD and location-cache buffers (the javadoc says this 'may be useful for parallel XPath evaluation'). VTDGen is per-parse state.

gotchas: parseFile(), parseGZIPFile() and similar catch IOException and ParseException, print them to System.out and return false. Use setDoc() + parse() if you need the exception.

Hard limits in VTDGen throw ParseException: depth 254, prefix 511 bytes, qualified name 2047 bytes, and 2 GB file size (1 GB with namespaces). Text tokens longer than 1M-1 bytes are split across several records.
The byte[] passed to setDoc() is the document. Records only point into it, so it must stay alive and unmodified for as long as the VTDNav is used.

toNormalizedString() collapses whitespace by design (issue #9); use toString(), or toRawString() to keep entities. Issue #6 reports toString() mishandling multibyte characters, with a fix promised for '2.13_2'.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only when you must stay on the JVM and want random access, a saved index or in-place byte edits. Every catalogued sibling is native: on the same bemayer page quick-xml's DOM Parse is faster than VTD-XML at every size, and RapidXml beats it at 1KB and 100MB. For XPath, prefer simdxml or libxml2 itself.
verified_claims_summary: On bemayer/xml-benchmark's 2026-09-01 run (GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest, Docker, CPU not published), VTD-XML 2.13.4 on Temurin 21 (no JVM flags, parse(false), input array cloned inside the timed loop) built its token index 1.6x-4.9x faster than Debian libxml2 2.9.14's xmlParseMemory + xmlFreeDoc (C++ harness, -O3) at 100KB-100MB. VTD-XML's rows cover only the wide file because it rejects the deep files, while libxml2's rows also average in a deep file it halts at depth 256; VTD-XML also loses at 1KB (2.8x) and on XPath //*[@id] at every size (6.8x-17x).
status_note: Abandoned: the last release is 2.13.4 (Maven Central, 2017) and the last commit on the maintainer's GitHub copy is 2018-06-28. The jar has no dependencies and is easy to adopt, but GPLv2 (commercial license on request), the listed US patents and a license-termination clause for parties in litigation with XimpleWare make it a legal-review item.
